compression.title: Crowd Counting Consortium
compression.lede: is a joint project of Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Connecticut, part of the Nonviolent Action Lab, that collects publicly available data on political protest events reported in the United States; Jeremy Pressman and Erica Chenoweth began it to count the Women’s March of 21 January 2017 (Ash Center page; maryleelabor record).

sentences.text: The Crowd Counting Consortium calls itself "A public interest and scholarly project to document protests and demonstrations in the United States." (Ash Center page), and the maryleelabor census enters it, under the names CCC and crowdcounting.org, as a public interest and scholarly project documenting protests and demonstrations in the United States and publishing an event dataset (maryleelabor record).

It is "a joint project of Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Connecticut that collects publicly available data on political protest events reported in the United States, including rallies, marches, demonstrations, and acts of civil disobedience" (Ash Center page; Policy Commons card), and in its blog's first post, of 9 February 2021, "a public-interest and scholarly project that documents political crowds in public spaces in the United States" (Counting Crowds); a third party's page on its 2025 data restates it as a Harvard and UConn project that has collected such data since January 2017, on events that "articulate grievances against or express support for political targets" (boB Rudis).

The census asks of it, as of every resource it enters, "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", answers in three fields it defines as whose record, who holds it and on what terms, and whether and how it keeps "minority positions, splits, expulsions and dissent", and places it in its area of labor action, "strikes, stoppages and protest events, counted and described" (maryleelabor record).

The question comes from the census's anchor, #1725, which found that "Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender" (#1725; maryleelabor record).

It "first emerged from a collaborative effort by Jeremy Pressman (UConn) and Erica Chenoweth (HKS) to estimate the number of participants in the Women’s March on Washington" on 21 January 2017, and has since expanded to near-real-time information on the occurrence, themes and scale of American protest (Ash Center page); its X account, linking crowdcounting.org, joined in February 2017, and the census dates its founding to 2017 (X; maryleelabor record).

It is part of the Nonviolent Action Lab at the Ash Center, which its blog calls "one of the two institutional pillars of this project, along with the University of Connecticut" (Ash Center page; Counting Crowds, 6 May 2024); its X profile states that it "is co-directed by @ ericachenoweth and @ djpressman" (X), its page lists a team of Chenoweth, Frank Stanton Professor of the First Amendment, Pressman, Senior Research Fellow, and others, a research associate of the consortium among them, and names Jay Ulfelder as the Lab's program director (Ash Center page), and the census records the operator as the two schools' joint project, part of the Lab, begun by Pressman and Chenoweth (maryleelabor record).

Its funding comes in part from foundations and university centres, the Freedom Together Foundation and the MacArthur Foundation among them, and earlier from the Carnegie Corporation of New York (Ash Center page), and the census names its holder "a university project (Harvard Kennedy School and UConn), funded by foundations and university centres; data published monthly on the Harvard Dataverse" (maryleelabor record).

It collects "publicly available data on political crowds reported in the United States, including marches, protests, demonstrations, riots, and other actions" and does not count crowds at meetings, teach-ins or academic workshops, panel discussions, fundraisers or town halls (Ash Center FAQ); the census's unit is "a political protest event reported in the United States, with crowd numbers", and its record object carries the same list, riots included, and the same exclusions (maryleelabor record).

The third party's page states the scope differently at one point: the dataset includes events "open to the public, free of charge, and nonviolent (not primarily organized to cause direct harm to persons)", in all U.S. states and territories with no minimum crowd size, virtual gatherings included and paid fundraisers, workshops, closed campaign events and routine government meetings excluded unless disrupted (boB Rudis); the consortium's own list includes riots (Ash Center FAQ).

That page's text carries, directly after its description of the dataset, the string "RetryClaude can make mistakes. Please double-check responses.", and states that its data run from January to May 2025, with its source on Codeberg (boB Rudis).

Its goal is "to make the aggregate data on crowd numbers publicly available for each event", collected in the public interest and for scholarly research (Ash Center FAQ), and the census records what it keeps as "the record of political crowds in the United States: occurrence, themes and scale, as publicly reported or submitted with a verifiable source" (maryleelabor record).

It has collaborated with countlove.org, "a volunteer group that developed a webcrawler to identify protests and demonstrations on a daily basis" (Ash Center page), a cooperation its X account marked in April 2022 (X), and the census calls its method news-derived event coding from public reports, verified public submissions and that webcrawler (maryleelabor record).

"We only post records that we can confirm and verify through fact-checking", a submission must carry "a source that is publicly verifiable", and "We will never post, release, or share identifying information that has not already been reported in the public domain." (Ash Center page); the University of Denver and the University of Connecticut determined that the project does not qualify as human subjects research (Ash Center FAQ), and the census carries the rules among its stated limits and the determinations as a negative tag (maryleelabor record).

Its data are published monthly on a publicly accessible Dataverse "for use by scholars, journalists, movement leaders, and others", in three phases, 2017–2020, 2021–2024 and 2025 to the present, with documentation and a citation form naming crowdcounting.org (Ash Center page); the About page of Counting Crowds, the "Blog of the Crowd Counting Consortium", has the data in monthly Google Sheets, a compiled and augmented version kept on GitHub by the Nonviolent Action Lab and updated weekly, usually on Wednesdays, and an interactive dashboard (Counting Crowds), and the census records its coverage as the United States from 2017 in the same three phases (maryleelabor record).

The census records public download from the Harvard Dataverse and a public submission form, no licence on the saved page, and as unchecked the dataset and its codebook, the licence, the crowdcounting.org site and the listed commentary (maryleelabor record).

Its X account wrote on 29 August 2024 "Since 2017, we've tallied 200,000 protests and rallies in the US...and counting." and on 3 July 2020 that it was closing in on 5,000 listings of antiracism protests (X); its commentary recorded nearly 2,300 protests on Palestine or Israel by 28 November 2023, "with hundreds of thousands of total participants", nearly 12,400 pro-Palestine and over 2,000 pro-Israel protests from 7 October 2023 to 7 June 2024, and protest at over 500 schools with encampments at more than 130 of them (Ash Center page), and its blog counted encampments on more than 100 campuses and at least 26 acts of civil disobedience or direct action on 15 April 2024 (Counting Crowds).

The census gives no total, the count "not stated as a total in the saved source" beyond that dated subset, and lists as holdings the three phases, the commentary, the Israel/Palestine dashboards and more than 600 scholarly citations (maryleelabor record).

Its page records the data's uses in public argument: the 2017 Women’s March as, at that time, the largest single-day demonstration in US history; the 2018 March for Our Lives and #Enough Walkouts as the broadest, in over 4,400 locations; the 2020 protests after George Floyd’s murder as the largest and broadest mobilization, in a New York Times analysis; the 2020 Black Lives Matter uprising as "overwhelmingly peaceful"; the 2023–2024 pro-Palestine protests as "generally peaceful", against common narratives of violence; the rebuttal of the narrative of "no resistance" to the second Trump administration, with "a high degree of nonviolent discipline among anti-Trump protesters"; and the No Kings protests of June and October 2025 among the largest single-day demonstrations in US history (Ash Center page).

Academics use the data to study protest, counter-protest and state response, the team's articles and essays have more than 600 scholarly citations, and the Nonviolent Action Lab publishes commentary on the data, the latest listed on the page dated 15 August 2025 (Ash Center page); the census's answers are how many protests on a theme occurred in a period and where, the size of named mobilizations, and whether a wave was broadly nonviolent, and its lifecycle and dates record an active project published monthly, its latest listed commentary 2025-08-15 (maryleelabor record).

On the census's question the record keeps the crowd: its losing side is "not recorded. The data are used to study protest, counter-protest and state response; the saved page shows nothing of the positions, splits or dissent inside the movements counted", the census tags it "NOT a labor dataset: it records political protest of every kind, and labor action only as part of it", and among what it does not answer it lists "the positions argued inside a movement, or which tendency organized an event" (maryleelabor record).

The census's own reading takes the dataset as "a holder independent of the movements and governments it counts, whose record has been used against prevailing narratives", which "keeps the crowd and leaves the internal argument of the movement unrecorded" (maryleelabor record).

#1725 states of its own case record that "no cross-organization dataset of left splits, or of minority positions later adopted, was found for any period", and that the frequency of its pattern across the left as a whole "is unmeasured" (#1725).

At its name, a new address queried with the census name on 31 October 2026, the Capture Registry records that the Overview gives the founders, institutional home, scope and data, "Faithful on founders, home and data.", with its founders and institutions named and the consortium's pages among six cards from Harvard, Counting Crowds (two), boB Rudis, Policy Commons and X, and records the resource as external to the archive (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The Registry reads the composition as putting 'nonviolent' first "in a scope the consortium states without it", against the page's "We collect publicly available data on political crowds reported in the United States" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31); the 'nonviolent' scope stands on the rail in the third party's page (boB Rudis).

The Registry also reads it as leaving out "the verification and privacy rules that bound the record", the fact-checking rule and the rule on identifying information, under the title "THE CONSORTIUM AT ITS GRAIN; ITS VERIFICATION AND PRIVACY RULES NOT CARRIED" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

Wikipedia has no article with the name; five articles mention it, among them Erica Chenoweth and Crowd counting, the article on the estimation of crowd sizes, which lists the consortium among its external links (Wikipedia).
